summary: NFL and CFL passer rating is what the Passer rating calculator works out, and it gets there from the passing attempts, the completions, the passing yards and the touchdowns. Think of it as a shortcut for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Passer rating calculator work?
sections.html:
The Passer rating calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports NFL and CFL passer rating in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the passing attempts, the completions, the passing yards and the touchdowns.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Passer rating calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

NFL and CFL passer rating=((50 ÷ 3) × (completions, passing attempts) + (50 ÷ 3) × (passing yards, passing attempts) + (50 ÷ 3) × (touchdowns, passing attempts) + (50 ÷ 3) × (interceptions, passing attempts))
A=(completions, passing attempts)
B=(passing yards, passing attempts)
C=(touchdowns, passing attempts)
D=(interceptions, passing attempts)
Interceptions=-1 ÷ 200 × passing attempts × NCAA passer rating + (1 ÷ 2) × completions + (21 ÷ 500) × passing yards + (33 ÷ 20) × touchdowns

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Passer rating calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the passing attempts, the completions and the passing yards — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Passer rating calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — passing attempts for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Passer rating calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns NFL and CFL passer rating, derived from the passing attempts, the completions and the passing yards. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Passer rating calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the passing attempts, the completions, the passing yards and the touchdowns, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Passer rating calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
